section_summary: This section covers occupation policy in Japan from late 1947 to early 1948. It includes a State–Army dispute over economic decentralization, reports on Japanese politics and press controls, a survey of women’s voting attitudes, and British commentary on the occupation, a peace settlement, and the Emperor.

subfiles.title: Letter on the draft cable concerning economic concentration
subfiles.to: Kenneth C. Royall, Secretary of the Army
subfiles.about: A State Department reply sends a revised cable and explains objections to the Army draft.
subfiles.summary: Requests further discussion of overall zaibatsu policy while urging immediate guidance to MacArthur on the ordinance.

subfiles.title: Commentary on proposed Army Department cable and State Department revisions
subfiles.about: State explains its proposed revisions to Army guidance on Japan’s economic decentralization ordinance.
subfiles.summary: The commentary defends mandatory action against excessive concentrations, objects to Army language on adverse price effects and priorities, and proposes longer appeal periods. It argues against Japanese judicial review, a compensation provision in this ordinance, and Washington review of implementing standards.

subfiles.title: Draft cable from War to SCAP
subfiles.about: Draft guidance lists changes required before passage of the economic concentration bill.
subfiles.summary: The draft revises definitions, findings, and appeal periods, and recommends industry-specific standards while allowing the ordinance to proceed.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1465: Conversation with Shigeru Nambara
subfiles.from: Acting Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards and summarizes a conversation with Tokyo University president Shigeru Nambara.
subfiles.summary: Nambara discusses a peace treaty, self-defense, communism, the purge, reparations, education, and Japan’s political leadership.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Shigeru Nambara
subfiles.about: Records Nambara’s views on Japan’s future and occupation policies.
subfiles.summary: Nambara favors an early peace treaty and limited Japanese self-defense, criticizes the breadth of the purge and some economic reforms, and prefers reparations from current production. He stresses education, describes communist influence in unions, and assesses leading political figures.

subfiles.title: Office memorandum on Akahata repatriation articles
subfiles.about: Notes SCAP’s consideration of prosecuting Akahata over articles on repatriation.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes the allegations and questions whether they clearly violate the Press Code.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1471: Proposed prosecution of Communist Party newspaper
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Reports possible prosecution of Akahata for its account of repatriation from Soviet-held areas.
subfiles.summary: Sebald forwards an article and the Press Code, saying SCAP views the newspaper’s allegations as distortions of its repatriation work.

subfiles.title: Akahata article: Aren’t Repatriation Ships Coming Yet?
subfiles.about: A repatriate blames Japanese government neglect for delays in transporting detainees from Nakhodka.
subfiles.summary: Tomoo Iinuma describes crowded camps, too few ships and supplies, poor shipboard food, and his view that Soviet authorities sought to speed repatriation.

subfiles.title: Press Code for Japan
subfiles.from: Office of the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Sets out ten occupation rules governing newspaper content.
subfiles.summary: Requires truthful reporting and restricts criticism, propaganda, and reporting on Allied troop movements.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2956: Daily Telegraph article on Japan
subfiles.from: Everett F. Drumright, American Embassy London
subfiles.about: Forwards Malcolm Muggeridge’s first account of occupied Japan.
subfiles.summary: Drumright notes Muggeridge’s uncertainty about how deeply occupation reforms have changed Japanese life.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Docile Apprenticeship in Democracy
subfiles.about: Assesses democratic reforms and Japanese responses to the occupation.
subfiles.summary: Muggeridge describes constitutional change, elections, women’s voting, the Emperor, war-crimes trials, and Japanese cooperation with occupation authorities. He questions whether outward compliance will become lasting democracy after MacArthur’s control ends.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1472: Study of women’s political attitudes
subfiles.from: Acting Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a SCAP report on women’s voting intentions.
subfiles.summary: Highlights lower reported political interest among women and stronger influence from husbands, especially in rural areas.

subfiles.title: The Mainichi Study of Women’s Political Attitudes
subfiles.from: SCAP Civil Information and Education Section
subfiles.about: Analyzes interviews with married couples before the April 1947 Diet election.
subfiles.summary: Researchers compared separate interviews with ballots completed later in Nakano, Ome, and Yuzurihara. Women initially expressed a party choice less often than men; after the second ballot, many more couples agreed, usually through wives moving toward husbands’ choices. The report relates stronger effects in rural communities to family structure and discusses limits of the study.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2990: Further Daily Telegraph article on Japan
subfiles.from: Everett F. Drumright, American Embassy London
subfiles.about: Forwards Muggeridge’s second article on MacArthur and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Notes its discussion of occupation programs and possible U.S. protection of Japan after occupation.

subfiles.title: Gen. MacArthur’s Faith in Japan’s Regeneration
subfiles.about: Profiles MacArthur and examines occupation policy and Japan’s strategic future.
subfiles.summary: Muggeridge describes MacArthur’s confidence in democratic reform, the purge, and the zaibatsu program. He reports a slower prospect for peace amid tensions involving China and the Soviet Union, and suggests that U.S. protection might follow the military occupation.

subfiles.title: Incoming telegram record
subfiles.about: Records receipt of a confidential incoming telegram.
subfiles.summary: The surviving OCR shows routing information but no readable message text.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 75: Times editorial on Japan
subfiles.from: Everett F. Drumright, American Embassy London
subfiles.about: Forwards the full Times editorial titled “New and Old Japan.”
subfiles.summary: Supplies the clipping for Department records following an earlier cable of excerpts.

subfiles.title: New and Old Japan
subfiles.about: Argues that economic decentralization and a supervised peace settlement could protect reforms in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The editorial welcomes passage of the decentralization bill and warns that established elites may regain influence. It favors ending occupation while binding Japan to reforms and retaining Allied supervision.

subfiles.title: Moscow airgram on Soviet criticism of U.S. policy in Japan
subfiles.about: Relays a Soviet article attacking U.S. occupation policy in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The readable passage accuses the United States of treating Japan as a colony and military base against the Soviet Union; much of the surrounding text is illegible.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 113: Third Daily Telegraph article on Japan
subfiles.from: Everett F. Drumright, American Embassy London
subfiles.about: Forwards Muggeridge’s final article on the Emperor.
subfiles.summary: Emphasizes Muggeridge’s conclusion that many Japanese still regard the Emperor as divine.

subfiles.title: With the Emperor in the Ruins of Hiroshima
subfiles.about: Examines the decision to retain the Emperor and describes his visit to Hiroshima.
subfiles.summary: Muggeridge presents arguments that retaining the Emperor enabled surrender and preserved administration, alongside concern that it sustained old beliefs. He describes the enthusiastic reception in Hiroshima and concludes that many Japanese still regard the Emperor as divine.
